title: Partial tagging flow for SDK ecosystem: safer release and rollforward
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Problem: emergency publish fixes and mistaken artifacts are currently handled by full rollbacks or ad-hoc yanking which is risky for downstream users and breaks traceability. We need a release flow that allows partial tagging (promote or demote specific language artifacts), reproducible provenance, and a safe rollforward path without forcing a global SDK rollback.
background: Over the past year weve increasingly encountered situations where only one language package (e.g., Python) needed a hotfix, but our release tooling and registry workflows favor atomic multi-language publishes. That leads to either republishing all packages (causing churn) or manual registry deletes that break provenance and audit trails. Existing related tickets focus on signed publishing and attestations, but none provide a minimal operator-friendly partial promotion and rollback story for multi-repo SDK bundles.
proposal:
Implement a partial tagging/promotion layer in the release pipeline that treats each language artifact as independently promotable through stages (draft -> staged -> public). Key pieces:
1) Add per-language release tags in CI (e.g., ruby:release/2026.04.01-py-1.2.3, ts:release/2026.04.01-ts-0.9.0) stored only in the release orchestration service until promoted.
2) Publish artifacts first to ephemeral registries (test.pypi / npm-staging / gocenter-staging) with signed SLSA-style attestations (Sigstore/cosign) and immutable checksums.
3) Provide a single API endpoint in release-orchestrator to promote a single artifact from staged to public which will: verify provenance, update canonical release manifest, push to public registries, and emit a signed promotion attestation.
4) Keep published metadata immutable; allow "deprecation" and "rollforward" via additional signed manifest entries instead of deleting artifacts to preserve traceability.
5) Expose a dashboard in Console to see per-language promotion status, attestation chain, and rollback/rollforward actions.
acceptance_criteria: 1) CI produces signed attestations for each language artifact on publish-to-staging. 2) Engineers can promote a single language artifact to public without republishing other languages. 3) Promotion action writes a signed entry to canonical release manifests stored in S3 and Git, and these records are verifiable offline. 4) Rollforward (publish corrected patch) does not require deleting the original artifact; manifests capture superseded versions and client-side pinning continues to work. 5) New flow is exercised by a canary release for Python and TypeScript SDKs in the next release cycle.
test_plan:
- Add unit tests for tag generation and manifest signing.
- End-to-end test in CI: publish Python to test.pypi, verify attestation, promote Python only, validate package visible in PyPI staging and public PyPI within allowed propagation window.
- Run compatibility tests for existing deploy scripts and sample apps.
- Manual smoke test: download older pinned SDK version after partial promotion to ensure no regressions.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: complexity in orchestration may introduce intermittent mismatches between manifest and registry state. Mitigation: implement idempotent promotion steps with verification checkpoints and retries; add alerting for failed promotions.\nRisk: registries with different semantics (PyPI vs npm vs Go) will need small per-registry adapters. Mitigation: build thin adapter interface and test adapters in staging.\nRisk: security approval needed for Sigstore integration. Mitigation: early engagement with security team and keep fallback of GPG-signed attestations until approved.
migration_steps: 1. Extend release-orchestrator schema to accept per-language artifacts and attestations
2. Add staging publish step to SDK CI workflows (python/ts/go) to push to ephemeral registries
3. Integrate cosign/Sigstore signing in CI and store attestations in artifacts-bucket
4. Implement promote endpoint and idempotent registry adapter logic
5. Add Console view and permission controls for promote/rollforward actions
6. Run litmus canary with internal SDK consumers then opt-in external customers
